newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-ASDA outperformance set to continue.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-ASDA outperformance set to continue.

text.p: British supermarket chain ASDA Group Plc rang up higher year profits and a strong sales performance on Thursday, prompting its shares to rise, with a promise it would continue to do better than its competitors.
"Do I believe that we can continue to outperform the industry? Yes, I do," Chief Executive Allan Leighton told Reuters in a telephone interview.

ASDA saw sales from existing stores up 9.2 percent in the year ending May 3 with pretax profits before exceptionals rising 16 percent to 353.7 million pounds ($588.1 million) and paid out a total dividend of 3.05 pence per share, up from 2.65 pence.
Its nearest rival on sales growth is market leader Tesco, which said earlier this month that sales were up 5.1 percent in the first 14 weeks of its financial year.
ASDA shares were boosted by the figures, gaining four pence to 126 pence, off an earlier high of 127 pence.
Analysts were reported to have raised profit forecasts for the year along with ratings for the stock.
"Sixty-two months of outperforming the industry is more than just a recovery," said Simon Dunn at Kleinwort Benson.
ASDA's entrepeneurial chairman Archie Norman, now a member of parliament for the opposition Conservative party, is largely credited for turning the company around from heavy losses five years ago.
"I don't see any slowdown in their momentum at the moment," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
"Management is very, very focused on delivering innovation and growth," Leighton told a press conference.
Plans to open five new stores this year and refurbish five others could create up to 4,000 jobs, Leighton said, with a new distribution centre likely to push up total new jobs to 5,000.

He said he was "sure we will be able to help" the new Labour government in its plans for a new deal to combat youth unemployment, which involves offering subsidies to employers who take on young jobless.
ASDA is known for its cheeky and innovative image and its reputation as a champion of consumers by breaking price monopolies.

On Thursday, it launched a team of "fashion police," who will hand out "fines" in the form of 10 percent discount vouchers to anyone wearing expensive or badly designed clothing as a promotion for ASDA's own "George" range.

Leighton said he felt the clothing business, sold under the "George" brand set up with George Davies who worked with Next Plc, could be twice the current size, which has seen sales rise 28 percent at existing stores.
"If I can sort the supply chain out...you can then generate a quality offer...at 20 percent of the price. That is a set of economics that nobody else can emulate," he said.

The company said its total market share increased to 11 percent from 10.1 percent a year ago as it focused on value for money over diversification into financial services like several of its competitors.
ASDA is the only one of Britain's big four supermarkets which does not offer a nationwide loyalty card and has not branched out into bank accounts or financial services.

Leighton, who took over as chief executive last year from Norman, said achieving such strong sales growth, "becomes more and more difficult," but added that he expected the company to outperform "not just on sales but on operating profit too."
Leighton said ASDA's operating margins were roughly flat last year along with gross margins as it reinvested revenues from higher margin products back into lower prices.
The company said in a statement that industry figures showed it was eight percent cheaper than its major competitors, which include market leader Tesco, J. Sainsbury and Safeway.
Leighton said it was a key measure that the gap "is maintained or increased versus our competitors."
ASDA focuses on large, out-of-town superstores where it can offer non-food items at discounts to high street stores, providing it with a unique selling opportunity.
"The only way in a very mature marketplace that you can outperform and generate real return is you've got to innovate faster than anybody else," Leighton said. ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
